beats.say: A to the power X plus one, over B to the power Y minus two, all squared,
asks: What does all squared cover?

beats.say: times B to the power X plus two, over A to the power three minus Y, equals A to the power nine B.
asks: Which part is the second fraction?

beats.say: Find X and Y. Two unknowns need two equations: the bases A and B give one each.
asks: How can one equation give two answers?
Why do the bases matter?

beats.say: The plan: tidy each side into one power of A times one power of B.
asks: What does one power of A mean?

beats.say: Then the powers of A must match, and the powers of B must match.
asks: Why must the powers match?

beats.say: Do the power first: the bracket must go before we can group the bases.
asks: Why do the power first?

beats.say: Squaring a fraction squares its top and its bottom.
asks: Does the square go to the top and bottom?

beats.say: Now times power: a power of a power, multiply the powers.
asks: Which law is this?

beats.say: Two times X plus one is two X plus two. Two times Y minus two is two Y minus four.
asks: Why multiply by two?
Why not write 2(x + 1) first?

beats.say: Put this back into the equation, next to the other fraction.
asks: Where does the rest of the line come from?

beats.say: Now group the same bases. Multiplying fractions: tops together, bottoms together.
asks: Why can I join the two fractions?

beats.say: Then divide. The same base is on top and bottom, so minus the powers: top power minus bottom power.
asks: Which law is this?
Why minus the powers?

beats.say: Keep the brackets: the whole bottom power is taken away.
asks: Why do I need the brackets?

beats.say: Now tidy each power. For A: two X plus two, minus the bracket three minus Y.
asks: Why tidy one power at a time?

beats.say: Minus a bracket flips every sign inside: the three becomes minus three, and minus Y becomes plus Y.
asks: Why does minus Y become plus Y?

do.text: Minus a bracket flips every sign inside

beats.say: For B: X plus two, minus the bracket two Y minus four.
asks: Which is the bottom power for b?

beats.say: Again every sign flips: minus two Y, and plus four.
asks: Why does minus four become plus four?

beats.say: Collect the terms: the left side is A to the power two X plus Y minus one,
asks: How do I collect the terms?

beats.say: times B to the power X minus two Y plus six.
asks: Where does the six come from?

beats.say: On the right, a bare B means B to the power one, so write it in.
asks: Why is b the same as b to the power 1?

beats.say: Now compare the powers of each base. First the base A.
asks: What does compare powers mean?

read: The equation is true for every value of $a$ and $b$.
Take $b = 1$: every power of $b$ is $1$, so only the $a$ parts are left.
Two powers of the same base are equal only when the powers are equal.
**Same base on both sides: the powers must match.**

beats.say: Since the base A is the same, the powers must be the same. Hence two X plus Y minus one equals nine.
asks: Why must the powers be the same?

beats.say: The base B is the same too, so its powers must be the same.
asks: Why are the b powers equal?

beats.say: Hence X minus two Y plus six equals one, the one from the bare B.
asks: Where did the 1 come from?

beats.say: Solve the two equations together: X equals three and Y equals four.
asks: How do I solve them together?
Can I check the answer?
